topic: The Secret Rhythm of Primes: From Dirichlet's Theorem to the Geometry of Pi
target_audience: Advanced high school students or undergraduate math enthusiasts

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Modulo Sorting Machine
lecture_lines: Imagine odd numbers flowing into a sorting machine.
We divide every number by four to find remainders.
This creates two distinct groups of numbers.
Gold bucket numbers leave a remainder of one.
Silver bucket numbers leave a remainder of three.
animations: Animation 1: A horizontal row of odd numbers (3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13) enters from the left screen edge.
Animation 2: A central processing box labeled 'Modulo 4' (#00FF00) appears in the middle of the screen.
Animation 3: Two containers appear: 'Gold Bucket (4k+1)' (#FFD700) on the left and 'Silver Bucket (4k+3)' (#C0C0C0) on the right.
Animation 4: The numbers 5, 9, and 13 move from the center and drop into the Gold Bucket.
Animation 5: The numbers 3, 7, and 11 move from the center and drop into the Silver Bucket.

sections.title: Dirichlet’s Discovery: Infinite Tracks
lecture_lines: These sequences form two infinite tracks for primes.
Primes like five and thirteen populate the gold track.
Primes like three and seven populate the silver track.
Dirichlet proved both tracks contain infinitely many primes.
No matter how far, prime runners never stop appearing.
animations: Animation 1: Two parallel horizontal lines representing 'Track 4k+1' (#FFD700) and 'Track 4k+3' (#C0C0C0) extend across the screen.
Animation 2: Prime numbers 5, 13, and 17 appear as gold dots along the top track.
Animation 3: Prime numbers 3, 7, 11, and 19 appear as silver dots along the bottom track.
Animation 4: The camera zooms out significantly, showing both tracks stretching into the infinite distance.
Animation 5: More dots pop up rapidly on both tracks, demonstrating an unending sequence of primes in both.

sections.title: The Prime Race: Chebyshev’s Bias
lecture_lines: A subtle race exists between these two infinite teams.
The silver team usually maintains a persistent lead.
This mysterious preference is called Chebyshev’s Bias.
animations: Animation 1: A digital scoreboard appears with labels 'Team 4k+1' (#FFD700) and 'Team 4k+3' (#C0C0C0).
Animation 2: Both counters rapidly increase to one million, with 'Team 4k+3' maintaining a slight, persistent lead.
Animation 3: The term 'Chebyshev’s Bias' (#00FFFF) appears in glowing text above the scoreboard to explain the lead.

sections.title: The Bridge to Pi: The Leibniz Connection
lecture_lines: These buckets bridge the gap between numbers and geometry.
We alternate fractions from each bucket in a series.
This algebraic pattern begins to construct a circle.
Positive and negative terms balance to find the area.
The infinite sum converges exactly to pi over four.
animations: Animation 1: The Leibniz formula '1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 +...' appears in white at the top of the screen.
Animation 2: Terms with denominator 4k+1 (1, 1/5) turn Gold (#FFD700); terms with denominator 4k+3 (1/3, 1/7) turn Silver (#C0C0C0).
Animation 3: Below the formula, a circle with radius 0.5 (Area = pi/4) begins to draw its outline.
Animation 4: Colored bars representing the terms add to and subtract from a visualization of the circle's area.
Animation 5: The jagged area visualization transforms into a perfectly smooth circle representing the sum pi/4.

sections.title: Synthesis: Order from Prime Chaos
lecture_lines: Prime distribution directly dictates the value of pi.
Algebraic rhythms transform into perfect geometric symmetry.
Primes define the very fabric of our mathematical world.
animations: Animation 1: The sorting buckets from Section 1 and the racing tracks from Section 2 reappear and overlap.
Animation 2: The tracks and buckets morph and bend together to form a large, glowing Pi symbol (#FF00FF).
Animation 3: The final text 'The Hidden Rhythm of Primes' appears beneath the Pi symbol.
